title: Ebola emerges

confidence.note: Both 1976 outbreaks were investigated on the spot by international teams, whose case counts are still cited. The Sudan figures cover the whole outbreak, not Nzara alone, and the cotton factory is a suspected rather than proven source. The two epidemics were caused by related but distinct viruses, a point not clear at the time.

place: Nzara, Sudan (now South Sudan), and Yambuku, Zaire (now Democratic Republic of the Congo)
people: Jean-Jacques Muyembe Tamfum, Congolese virologist who took early samples at Yambuku
Peter Piot, Belgian microbiologist whose Antwerp laboratory isolated the virus
summary: In 1976 a new hemorrhagic fever struck southern Sudan and a Congolese mission hospital, where five syringes a day spread it from patient to patient.
body: In 1976 a deadly new hemorrhagic fever appeared twice, in two places. In southern Sudan an outbreak spread through four towns and was traced to Nzara, where a cotton factory is suspected as the source; 151 of 284 recorded patients died. In Yambuku, in northern Zaire, a mission hospital issued only five syringes a day; reused needles carried the virus to outpatients, and 280 of 318 cases died. The Congolese doctor Jean-Jacques Muyembe took early blood samples bare-handed, and Peter Piot's Antwerp laboratory isolated the virus from a nun's blood. The disease was named for a nearby river. The two outbreaks involved related but distinct viruses.

links.note: The same virus returned on a vastly larger scale in 2014.
Another virus out of central Africa that reshaped global health.

title: Smallpox is eradicated

confidence.note: WHO records date the intensified campaign (1967), the last natural case (Somalia, October 1977), certification (9 December 1979) and the formal declaration (May 1980). How much credit belongs to surveillance-containment rather than continued mass vaccination is a matter of emphasis, not of fact.

place: Worldwide; last natural case at Merca, Somalia
people: William Foege, former CDC epidemiologist working as a missionary, who used surveillance and containment in eastern Nigeria
Rahima Banu, of Bangladesh, the last known case of *Variola major* (1975)
Ali Maow Maalin, of Merca, Somalia, the last naturally transmitted case (1977)
Janet Parker (d. 1978), medical photographer in Birmingham, the last known person to contract smallpox, in a laboratory-linked outbreak
summary: A disease that killed some 300 million people in the 20th century alone was hunted to extinction village by village. It remains the only human disease ever eradicated.
body: Smallpox killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone. In 1967 the World Health Organization launched an intensified eradication campaign, and thirteen years later its member states declared the disease gone. It remains the only human disease ever eradicated.

The original plan was to vaccinate at least 80 percent of populations and rely on herd immunity. Vaccine shortages changed the strategy. In eastern Nigeria in 1967–1968, during the Biafran war, William Foege, a former CDC epidemiologist then working as a missionary, vaccinated the families and close contacts of each patient, and watched outbreaks melt away. This approach, called surveillance and containment and later ring vaccination, became the backbone of the campaign: find every case, vaccinate everyone around it. In India alone more than 150,000 field workers searched for cases.

The disease retreated to the Horn of Africa. The last natural case of the deadlier *Variola major* was Rahima Banu, in Bangladesh, in 1975; the last naturally transmitted case of all was Ali Maow Maalin, in Merca, Somalia, on 26 October 1977. A Global Commission certified eradication on 9 December 1979, and in May 1980 the World Health Assembly declared that the world and all its peoples had won freedom from smallpox.

One more death came from a laboratory. In 1978 Janet Parker, a medical photographer in Birmingham, England, caught smallpox while working a floor above a laboratory that handled the virus, and died; she is regarded as the last person to contract the disease. How she was infected remains a matter of conjecture. Samples of the virus survive at two designated laboratories, one in the United States and one in Russia, which is why eradication did not end the debate about smallpox.

myth.tradition: Ring vaccination was a brand-new idea invented for the eradication campaign, and it replaced mass vaccination.
myth.record: Isolating cases had precedents, from the Leicester method of 1877 (notification, isolation and quarantine) to an expanding-ring vaccination of contacts in Libya in 1946. In the campaign itself mass vaccination continued; what changed was that resources shifted toward finding cases and containing them.

links.note: Jenner's cowpox vaccine, refined over 170 years, was the tool.
The success inspired the next eradication attempt.
Health for All was declared as the smallpox campaign ended.

title: The first IVF baby

confidence.note: Louise Brown's birth and the Edwards–Steptoe method are fully documented, including in their own 1978 report. Jean Purdy's share was long underplayed and has been reassessed from the laboratory notebooks; the Calcutta birth of Durga is now widely credited in India but rests on Subhas Mukhopadhyay's own reports, reviewed only in 1997.

place: Oldham, near Manchester, England (where the IVF treatment was carried out)
people: Robert Edwards, born 1925, Cambridge physiologist, Nobel Prize 2010
Patrick Steptoe (d. 1988), Oldham gynecologist and laparoscopy pioneer
Jean Purdy (d. 1985), Edwards's laboratory and clinical partner, who kept most of the records
Louise Brown (b. 1978), the first baby born after IVF
Subhas Mukhopadhyay (1931–1981), Calcutta physiologist who reported India's first IVF birth
summary: After a decade of failures, funding refusals and public alarm, a baby conceived in a laboratory dish was born in Oldham in July 1978. Millions have followed.
body: On 25 July 1978 a healthy girl, Louise Brown, was delivered by Caesarean section after IVF treatment carried out at Oldham, in northern England. Her parents, Lesley and John Brown, had tried for nine years to have a child. She had been conceived in a laboratory dish, not a test tube, and returned to her mother's womb as an eight-cell embryo.

The work behind her began in the 1950s, when the Cambridge physiologist Robert Edwards set out to learn how human eggs mature and when they can be fertilized. In 1969 he achieved fertilization of a human egg outside the body, but the embryos would not develop. He teamed up with Patrick Steptoe, an Oldham gynecologist who could collect ripe eggs with the laparoscope, then a new and controversial instrument. The Medical Research Council declined to fund the project, a private donation kept it alive, and religious leaders, ethicists and scientists demanded that it stop.

A third partner was long left out of the story. Jean Purdy kept most of the records, helped care for patients and probably spent more time in Oldham than Edwards did. In 1980–81 Edwards argued with hospital administrators that a commemorative plaque should name her. Purdy died of cancer in 1985 and Steptoe in 1988, so when the Nobel Prize came in 2010, Edwards was the only one of the three still alive to receive it.

There may also have been a near-rival. On 3 October 1978 a Calcutta team led by Subhas Mukhopadhyay announced the birth of a girl, Durga, by IVF. A West Bengal government committee with no expertise in IVF dismissed his work as bogus; he was transferred, kept from research, and took his own life in 1981. His work was recognized only after T. C. Anand Kumar re-examined it in 1997.
By 2010 about four million people had been born after IVF, including children of Louise Brown herself.

myth.tradition: Louise Brown was a "test-tube baby", conceived in a test tube.
myth.record: Fertilization took place in a shallow culture dish, as the Nobel committee itself notes, and the Oldham work was a three-person effort: Jean Purdy's role, the laboratory notebooks show, was substantial.

links.note: Steptoe's laparoscope was the key to collecting eggs.
Human embryonic stem cells came from IVF embryos.
Hormonal control of reproduction, from the other direction.

title: Health for All: the Alma-Ata Declaration

confidence.note: The declaration text and conference report are WHO documents. Its long-term influence is debated; the selective primary health care counter-proposal of 1979 is well documented.

place: Alma-Ata, Kazakh SSR, USSR (now Almaty, Kazakhstan)
people: Halfdan Mahler, WHO Director-General
James Grant, UNICEF executive director
summary: In 1978 the world's governments promised health for all by the year 2000 through community primary care. Within a year major donors were proposing a narrower, more cost-effective plan.
body: In September 1978 delegates met in Alma-Ata, in Soviet Kazakhstan, and declared health a fundamental human right. Primary health care, close to where people live and work, was to bring an acceptable level of health to all the people of the world by the year 2000. The backlash came fast. At Bellagio in 1979, UNICEF's James Grant joined the World Bank, USAID and the Rockefeller Foundation in promoting selective primary health care: a few targeted interventions, later known as GOBI (growth monitoring, oral rehydration, breastfeeding, immunization), which shifted emphasis away from community health worker programs.

title: AIDS

confidence.note: The first report (5 June 1981) and the 1983 virus discovery are documented in print. The virus's origin in Kinshasa around 1920 is a statistical estimate from viral genetics, with a range of roughly 1909–1930; priority for the discovery was bitterly disputed between Paris and the US National Cancer Institute.

place: Los Angeles and New York, USA; Paris, France; origins in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo
people: Françoise Barré-Sinoussi (b. 1947), Pasteur Institute virologist, Nobel Prize 2008
Luc Montagnier (1932–2022), Pasteur Institute virologist, Nobel Prize 2008
Robert Gallo (b. 1937), US National Cancer Institute, rival claimant to the discovery
summary: Five cases of a rare pneumonia in Los Angeles in 1981 were the first sign of a pandemic that had begun in central Africa decades earlier and has killed over 44 million people.
body: On 5 June 1981 the US Centers for Disease Control's weekly bulletin reported five unexplained cases of *Pneumocystis* pneumonia in previously healthy gay men at three Los Angeles hospitals. Reports of a rare cancer, Kaposi's sarcoma, followed from New York. Within a year the CDC had 355 cases of such illnesses in previously healthy people.

The early link to gay men shaped everything. Newspapers wrote of a "gay cancer" and doctors of "gay-related immune deficiency", tying the disease to stigmatized behavior. Soon it was also found in hemophiliacs, blood-transfusion recipients, drug users and infants.

In 1983 Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier at the Pasteur Institute in Paris isolated a new retrovirus from a patient's swollen lymph node. In April 1984 the US government announced that Robert Gallo's laboratory had isolated a candidate virus, HTLV-III, opening a scientific and legal battle over credit. The 2008 Nobel Prize went to the Paris pair.

The virus was far older than the disease. Genetic analysis places the common ancestor of the pandemic strain around 1920, in Kinshasa, and blood samples from Kinshasa in 1959–1960 already contain it. By one estimate it reached Haiti in the mid-1960s and the United States around 1969, a dozen years before anyone noticed.

Activists, among them ACT UP, founded in New York in 1987, turned people facing a lethal, stigmatized disease and an unresponsive government into caregivers, advocates and "citizen scientists". The World Health Organization now estimates that HIV has claimed 44.2 million lives, and that 41 million people were living with it at the end of 2025.

myth.tradition: AIDS began in the United States around 1981.
myth.record: 1981 is when doctors first recognized the syndrome. The virus had been spreading from Kinshasa since about the 1920s and had probably been in the United States since the late 1960s.

title: A vaccine against a cancer

confidence.note: The 1981 US licensing and the 1986 recombinant vaccines are well documented. The link between vaccination and Taiwan's later fall in liver cancer rests on population registry data rather than a trial, and the cited analysis says the decrease 'may be attributed' to the program, so the cancer claim is rated agreed rather than firm.

people: Baruch Blumberg, American geneticist, Nobel Prize 1976
Irving Millman, Blumberg's co-inventor of the vaccine
summary: A puzzling blood protein called Australia antigen led to the hepatitis B vaccine, and in Taiwan to a later fall in liver cancer that researchers attribute to vaccination.
body: Baruch Blumberg was studying inherited blood-protein variation when an unknown protein turned up in tests of a transfused hemophilia patient's serum against blood from an Aboriginal Australian. Between 1966 and 1968 he showed that this "Australia antigen" went with hepatitis B; it proved to be the virus's outer coat. Healthy carriers' blood was full of these non-infectious particles, and Blumberg and Irving Millman made a vaccine from them. The US approved a plasma-derived version in 1981; genetically engineered vaccines followed in 1986. Taiwan began vaccinating infants of infected mothers in 1984 and all infants in 1986, and liver cancer later fell, a decline attributed in part to the program.

title: Ulcers are an infection

confidence.note: Warren's first sighting (1979), the joint study and culture (1982) and the Lancet papers (1983–84) are documented; the self-experiment's timing rests on Marshall's own account. That the bacterium causes most peptic ulcers is now settled.

place: Royal Perth Hospital and Fremantle Hospital, Western Australia
people: J. Robin Warren, born 1937, Perth pathologist
Barry Marshall, born 1951, Perth physician
summary: Two Perth doctors argued that stomach ulcers were caused by a bacterium, not stress. One infected himself to prove the point; official acceptance took a decade.
body: In 1979, on his 42nd birthday, the Perth pathologist Robin Warren noticed curved bacteria on a stomach biopsy, always alongside inflammation. In 1981 the young physician Barry Marshall joined him, and in 1982 they cultured the organism, now called *Helicobacter pylori*, finding it in almost all patients with gastritis or ulcers. At the time ulcers were blamed on stress and lifestyle, and treated by suppressing acid; they often came back.

Their papers met disbelief. In 1984, unable to infect animals, Marshall deliberately infected himself; his own biopsies showed colonization and the typical damage to the stomach lining. Others soon replicated the findings, and treatment trials showed that ulcers stayed healed once the bacteria were eradicated. Formal acceptance came only in 1994, when a US National Institutes of Health consensus meeting endorsed detecting and eradicating the infection. Warren and Marshall shared the 2005 Nobel Prize.

myth.tradition: A lone maverick swallowed bacteria and overturned medical dogma overnight.
myth.record: Warren saw the bacteria first, other groups confirmed the findings from 1983, and Marshall himself called reports that he was alone exaggerated. Acceptance took about ten years and rested on treatment trials.

links.note: Marshall's self-infection was an attempt to satisfy Koch's postulates.
The stomach turned out not to be sterile.

title: PCR

confidence.note: The 1983 conception rests on Mullis's own recollection; the first publication (1985) and the Taq method (1988) are firm. Credit is contested: Kleppe proposed the principle in 1971, and Cetus colleagues made the method work.

people: Kary Mullis, Cetus chemist, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1993
Kjell Kleppe, Norwegian biochemist who proposed the principle in 1971
Thomas D. Brock, microbiologist who found *Thermus aquaticus*
summary: A chemist's idea on a night drive became a way to copy a single stretch of DNA millions of times in a few hours, transforming diagnosis, forensics and genetics.
body: One night in 1983, driving from Berkeley to his cabin in Mendocino, the Cetus chemist Kary Mullis saw how two short primers flanking a stretch of DNA could let a polymerase copy it, and the copies be copied again, doubling the amount each cycle. Repeated cycle after cycle, the process yields millions of copies in a few hours.

The idea was not wholly new: in 1971 Kjell Kleppe had proposed amplifying DNA between two primers, but the idea was not realized. It took numerous adjustments by Mullis's colleagues at Cetus to make the method work; it was published in 1985. Its breakthrough came with a heat-tolerant polymerase from *Thermus aquaticus*, a bacterium Thomas Brock had found in Yellowstone's hot springs in 1969, which survived the heating step (1988). PCR made it possible to detect HIV and inherited mutations, analyze traces of DNA from crime scenes and sequence the human genome. Mullis won the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

myth.tradition: Kary Mullis invented PCR single-handedly in a flash of inspiration.
myth.record: The principle had been described in 1971, and the working method, including the switch to heat-stable Taq polymerase, came from a team at Cetus.

links.note: Base pairing between complementary strands is what PCR exploits.
Sequencing the genome depended on amplification.
PCR became a standard test for HIV.
